title: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval: A Static Value Prior Reverses the Gap

paper.title: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval: A Static Value Prior Reverses the Gap
paper.abstract: Abstract. Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR’s measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still underperforms a 47 × 47\times smaller dense encoder. Our code and artifacts are open-sourced at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gr-dr-release-BCE4.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Dense retrieval (DR) has long been a standard candidate-generation approach for recommendation. It encodes a user’s interaction history and catalog items in a shared embedding space, then retrieves nearby items ( Covington et al., 2016 ; Yi et al., 2019 ) . Advances in language models and semantic IDs have made generative retrieval (GR) an increasingly viable alternative. GR represents items with semantic IDs and generates the next item’s ID one token at a time ( De Cao et al., 2021 ; Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ) . Recent work has demonstrated GR at industrial scale ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zhou and others, 2025a ; Zhou and others, 2025b ) , but its use does not establish that it consistently outperforms or can replace DR in candidate generation. As shown in Fig. 1 , normally DR retrieves the held out next item more often, while GR’s best relevant item has higher value on average for users both methods cover. Figure 1. GR and DR use the same user history but generate candidates through semantic ID decoding and dense search. GR leads on best item value, while DR leads on exact target retrieval and full list value. A static prior reranks DR candidates and moves the potential valuable item into the top k k . The apparent winner depends on how retrieval is evaluated. This metric choice is particularly crucial in e-commerce candidate generation, where retrieved products differ not only in relevance to the user but also its commercial value. To understand why, we need to know whether GR’s value lead comes from the user’s history or from generally valuable items. Recall and target NDCG show whether the held out item is retrieved and where it ranks. They do not account for other relevant items, their ranks, or their value. To understand the disagreement, in this paper, we measure both the best relevant item and relevant value across the full list. We apply these metrics in controlled GR and DR comparisons on Amazon Toys 2014 and 2023 ( McAuley et al., 2015 ; He and McAuley, 2016 ; Hou et al., 2024 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . The metric disagreement persists on both public e-commerce datasets. From analysis, popularity is the largest component of GR’s measured value lead. Among users where GR wins, popularity contributes 49.8% of its value lead on 2014 and 65.4% on 2023. Reranking DR with the static item value score reverses the best item value gap while preserving a recall lead over GR. Further checks with cold targets, substitute credit, a random control, and graded industrial relevance do not reveal a consistent GR advantage. Our main contributions are: • We define complementary metrics for sequential recommendation in e-commerce scenario and show that they favor different methods in the GR and DR comparison. • We decompose GR’s measured value lead and find that popularity is its largest component on both public datasets. • We propose a training-free value prior, applied to DR as a single rerank of its retrieval results. This reverses GR’s lead in best relevant item value while preserving DR’s recall lead.

sections.heading: The Generative Turn for Retrieval Systems
sections.text: Prior to decoder-only approaches, sequential recommendation models for retrieval have been prevalent in production ( Covington et al., 2016 ; Yi et al., 2019 ) . The canonical dense retrieval (DR) is therefore defined as bidirectional sequential models for next-item prediction ( Hidasi et al., 2016 ; Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) . Generative retrieval (GR) enters the foreground as a constrained autoregressive decoding mechanism to generative identifier tokens, semantic IDs (SIDs), mappable to an underlying item, whose codebook construction follows RQ-VAE ( De Cao et al., 2021 ; Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ) . SID generative retrieval benefits from the rise of LLMs and demonstrates generalization, establishing itself for industry applications ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zhou and others, 2025a ; Zhou and others, 2025b ) . Note that GR umbrellas non-SID approaches such as P5 and HSTU ( Geng et al., 2022 ; Zhai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Our controlled DR-GR comparison is grounded on LIGER, while research on GR’s scaling difficulties and DR’s capacity limits bounds our conclusions without determining them ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Pradeep et al., 2023 ; Weller et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Difficulty of Retrieval Evaluation
sections.text: Offline recommendation evaluation suffers from sensitivity to missing feedback, candidate sampling and temporal splitting decisions ( Steck, 2010 ; Cremonesi et al., 2010 ; Krichene and Rendle, 2020 ; Cañamares and Castells, 2020 ; Dallmann et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2023 ) . Audits on these decisions reveal that they can change recommendation rankings, while recent studies identify GR artifacts from SID collision and benchmark shortcuts ( Ferrari Dacrema et al., 2019 ; Hidasi and Czapp, 2023 ; Sun, 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Our contribution identifies substitute non-identifiability under exact-target metrics and show how it worsens with catalog scale.

sections.heading: Popularity Bias is a Static Prior
sections.text: In recommendation, popularity of certain products are deeply associated with benchmark accuracy ( Steck, 2011 ; Jannach et al., 2015 ) . However, popularity also presents itself as a bias that degrades exposure and fairness for non-popular items ( Abdollahpouri et al., 2019 ; Klimashevskaia et al., 2024 ) . Popularity bias in GR becomes prominent due to inherent bias within LLMs ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . While these works mitigate popularity bias, our result show that under a same model GR-DR comparison, the advantage from popularity is replaceable by a user-independent prior that can be transferred to DR without decoding.

sections.heading: Problem Definition
sections.text: In the e-commerce setting, for each user u u , let h u = ( i 1 , … , i t ) h_{u}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{t}) denote the observed user product interaction history and y u = i t + 1 y_{u}=i_{t+1} the held out next item. A candidate generator x x uses h u h_{u} to produce the ranked list L x k ​ ( u ) = ( i x , u ( 1 ) , … , i x , u ( k ) ) , L_{x}^{k}(u)=\bigl(i_{x,u}^{(1)},\ldots,i_{x,u}^{(k)}\bigr), where i x , u ( j ) i_{x,u}^{(j)} is the item at rank j j .

sections.heading: Models
sections.text: We compare GR and DR using the TIGER and LIGER framework ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Both arms use the same interaction data, item catalog, and jointly trained T5 encoder decoder. GR decodes valid semantic IDs through prefix constrained beam search, while DR ranks items by cosine similarity using the encoder representation of the same history. Thus, the arms differ mainly in their retrieval readout.

sections.heading: Datasets
sections.text: Our public evaluation uses the 2014 and 2023 releases of Amazon Toys. The 2014 dataset contains 11,924 items and 19,412 user histories under a leave last out split. Among their held out targets, 19,116 were seen during training and 296 were absent from training. Our results reproduce the LIGER Recall@10 values, while our GR recall exceeds the published TIGER result. The 2023 catalog is 13.6 × 13.6\times larger, which tests whether the observed pattern and the proposed intervention survive a substantial increase in catalog scale ( Hou et al., 2024 ) . We transfer the value weights and reranking coefficient from 2014 to 2023 without change unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 4. Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We compare GR and DR by asking which retrieved items are relevant and how much value they carry . A relevance labeling rule q u ​ ( i ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q_{u}(i)\in[0,1] assigns evaluation credit after ranking and is not a model score. It may credit only the held-out item, include substitute candidates, or assign partial credit through graded judgments. In contrast, v i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] v_{i}\in[0,1] measures a static property of item i i . For any rule q q , the relevant set with k k candidates is defined as R x k ​ ( u , q ) = { i ∈ L x k ​ ( u ) ∣ q u ​ ( i ) > 0 } . R_{x}^{k}(u;q)=\{i\in L_{x}^{k}(u)\mid q_{u}(i)>0\}. This definition keeps relevance and item value separate across evaluation protocols. In this section, We first define exact-target and category-based relevance, then introduce static catalog value, and finally combine them at the best-item and whole-list levels.

NDCG@ k k evaluates the same target with a rank discount ( Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002 ) . Both metrics measure recovery of the observed next interaction and give no credit to other potentially useful items.

sections.heading: 5. From Metric Dependency to a Static Prior
sections.text: We now apply these complementary metrics in a three-step analysis. We first show that GR leads on BV while DR leads on vNDCG \mathrm{vNDCG} . sections.heading: 5.2. Diagnosing GR’s Value Advantage
sections.text: Among users where GR wins BV \mathrm{BV} , we use Equation 1 to break its value lead over DR into popularity, rating, and brand. Popularity contributes for 49.8% of the lead on 2014 and 65.4% on 2023. It is the largest component on both datasets, and its share is higher on the larger 2023 catalog. Rating and brand contribute the remainder, but neither provides the same cross-dataset dominance. This pattern narrows the interpretation of GR’s value edge. Each value component is computed once per item and does not depend on the current history. The measured lift is therefore largely captured by static item-level properties, especially popularity. Repeated exposure in training offers a possible explanation for GR’s value lead. The released 2014 popularity score correlates with how often held out targets appear in training histories (Spearman ρ = 0.582 \rho=0.582 ). At least ten training histories contain 50.3% of held out targets in 2014 and 75.1% in 2023. GR may learn a preference for frequently seen items while predicting their semantic IDs. This could contribute to its lead because popularity is part of the item value score. That statement yields a falsifiable implication. If static item properties account for the operational advantage, then explicitly adding the same information to DR should reproduce it without autoregressive decoding.

sections.heading: 6. Robustness Beyond Exact-Match Evaluation
sections.text: The public results show that the item prior closes GR’s value gap. We now test whether GR does better on cold targets or when useful alternatives to the held out target receive credit. For the latter, we use public substitute evidence and graded judgments on an industrial recommendation dataset.

sections.heading: 6.1. Cold Items
sections.text: We test whether generation helps retrieve targets absent from interaction training. GR finds none of 296 cold targets on 2014 and 5 of 1,899 on 2023. DR finds 47 and 27, while DR+prior finds 36 and 21, respectively. Both DR methods find more cold targets than GR on each dataset.

sections.heading: 6.2. Substitute Credit and Graded Relevance
sections.text: An exact target miss does not tell us whether a list contains a useful alternative. For the median user, the held out target has 157 same-leaf alternatives on 2014 and 1,046 on 2023, a 6.7 × 6.7\times increase. Among DR’s 8,635 exact target misses on 2014, 58.2% include an item from that category in the top 50 while the target ranks beyond 200. In another 25.7%, the target ranks between 50 and 200. GR finds the exact target in only 748 of these DR misses, so the misses alone do not show an advantage for GR. We give binary credit to items linked to the target in Amazon co purchase data, which is reported in Table 2 . In this test, a 0.0447 lead for DR under exact Recall@50 becomes a 0.0183 lead for GR. For the binary test, randomly chosen items given the same amount of credit move the gap at least as far toward GR. With graded NDCG, DR leads again by 0.0153. The binary reversal therefore does not establish that GR retrieves better alternatives. Leaf category overlap and co-purchase links are imperfect evidence of usefulness. sections.heading: 6.3. Industrial LLM-Judged Relevance
sections.text: The industrial evaluation uses real e-commerce interaction histories and a product catalog. GR uses a Qwen3 14B model that generates semantic IDs, while DR uses a GTE encoder with about 300 million parameters. GR has roughly 47 × 47\times as many parameters. A substitute-aware LLM judge calibrated with 250 human labels scores each candidate’s relevance from zero to one, allowing partial credit for useful alternatives. Because the models differ in backbone and size, this evaluation tests whether the public result also holds in this setting. It cannot isolate the effect of retrieval architecture. sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we revisited the GR and DR in a controlled e-commerce comparison and we find two distinct parts to GR’s measured advantage. First, metric choice changes the apparent winner. GR leads on the value of the best relevant item, while DR leads on exact target recall and relevant value across the ranked list on both public datasets. Second, popularity makes the largest contribution to GR’s value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this gap while preserving DR’s recall lead. Cold target and substitute credit checks do not reveal a broader GR advantage. Graded judgments on an industrial dataset place DR above a larger GR model and DR with the prior above both. These results make DR with a static value prior a useful baseline for future GR systems.

Affiliation: Shopify Affiliation: University of Toronto , Yang Liu Affiliation: Shopify and Shuying Sun Note: Corresponding author: shuying.sun@shopify.com . Affiliation: Shopify 2026 Abstract. Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR’s measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still underperforms a 47 × 47\times smaller dense encoder. Our code and artifacts are open-sourced at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gr-dr-release-BCE4. Keywords: generative retrieval, dense retrieval, sequential recommendation, semantic IDs, popularity bias, recommendation evaluation 1. Introduction Dense retrieval (DR) has long been a standard candidate-generation approach for recommendation. It encodes a user’s interaction history and catalog items in a shared embedding space, then retrieves nearby items ( Covington et al., 2016 ; Yi et al., 2019 ) . Advances in language models and semantic IDs have made generative retrieval (GR) an increasingly viable alternative. GR represents items with semantic IDs and generates the next item’s ID one token at a time ( De Cao et al., 2021 ; Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ) . Recent work has demonstrated GR at industrial scale ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zhou and others, 2025a ; Zhou and others, 2025b ) , but its use does not establish that it consistently outperforms or can replace DR in candidate generation. As shown in Fig. 1 , normally DR retrieves the held out next item more often, while GR’s best relevant item has higher value on average for users both methods cover. Figure 1. GR and DR use the same user history but generate candidates through semantic ID decoding and dense search. GR leads on best item value, while DR leads on exact target retrieval and full list value. A static prior reranks DR candidates and moves the potential valuable item into the top k k . The apparent winner depends on how retrieval is evaluated. This metric choice is particularly crucial in e-commerce candidate generation, where retrieved products differ not only in relevance to the user but also its commercial value. To understand why, we need to know whether GR’s value lead comes from the user’s history or from generally valuable items. Recall and target NDCG show whether the held out item is retrieved and where it ranks. They do not account for other relevant items, their ranks, or their value. To understand the disagreement, in this paper, we measure both the best relevant item and relevant value across the full list. We apply these metrics in controlled GR and DR comparisons on Amazon Toys 2014 and 2023 ( McAuley et al., 2015 ; He and McAuley, 2016 ; Hou et al., 2024 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . The metric disagreement persists on both public e-commerce datasets. From analysis, popularity is the largest component of GR’s measured value lead. Among users where GR wins, popularity contributes 49.8% of its value lead on 2014 and 65.4% on 2023. Reranking DR with the static item value score reverses the best item value gap while preserving a recall lead over GR. Further checks with cold targets, substitute credit, a random control, and graded industrial relevance do not reveal a consistent GR advantage. Our main contributions are: • We define complementary metrics for sequential recommendation in e-commerce scenario and show that they favor different methods in the GR and DR comparison. • We decompose GR’s measured value lead and find that popularity is its largest component on both public datasets. • We propose a training-free value prior, applied to DR as a single rerank of its retrieval results. This reverses GR’s lead in best relevant item value while preserving DR’s recall lead. 2. Related Work The Generative Turn for Retrieval Systems Prior to decoder-only approaches, sequential recommendation models for retrieval have been prevalent in production ( Covington et al., 2016 ; Yi et al., 2019 ) . The canonical dense retrieval (DR) is therefore defined as bidirectional sequential models for next-item prediction ( Hidasi et al., 2016 ; Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) . Generative retrieval (GR) enters the foreground as a constrained autoregressive decoding mechanism to generative identifier tokens, semantic IDs (SIDs), mappable to an underlying item, whose codebook construction follows RQ-VAE ( De Cao et al., 2021 ; Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ) . SID generative retrieval benefits from the rise of LLMs and demonstrates generalization, establishing itself for industry applications ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zhou and others, 2025a ; Zhou and others, 2025b ) . Note that GR umbrellas non-SID approaches such as P5 and HSTU ( Geng et al., 2022 ; Zhai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Our controlled DR-GR comparison is grounded on LIGER, while research on GR’s scaling difficulties and DR’s capacity limits bounds our conclusions without determining them ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Pradeep et al., 2023 ; Weller et al., 2026 ) . Difficulty of Retrieval Evaluation Offline recommendation evaluation suffers from sensitivity to missing feedback, candidate sampling and temporal splitting decisions ( Steck, 2010 ; Cremonesi et al., 2010 ; Krichene and Rendle, 2020 ; Cañamares and Castells, 2020 ; Dallmann et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2023 ) . Audits on these decisions reveal that they can change recommendation rankings, while recent studies identify GR artifacts from SID collision and benchmark shortcuts ( Ferrari Dacrema et al., 2019 ; Hidasi and Czapp, 2023 ; Sun, 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Our contribution identifies substitute non-identifiability under exact-target metrics and show how it worsens with catalog scale. Popularity Bias is a Static Prior In recommendation, popularity of certain products are deeply associated with benchmark accuracy ( Steck, 2011 ; Jannach et al., 2015 ) . However, popularity also presents itself as a bias that degrades exposure and fairness for non-popular items ( Abdollahpouri et al., 2019 ; Klimashevskaia et al., 2024 ) . Popularity bias in GR becomes prominent due to inherent bias within LLMs ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . While these works mitigate popularity bias, our result show that under a same model GR-DR comparison, the advantage from popularity is replaceable by a user-independent prior that can be transferred to DR without decoding. 3. Controlled Comparison Setup Problem Definition In the e-commerce setting, for each user u u , let h u = ( i 1 , … , i t ) h_{u}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{t}) denote the observed user product interaction history and y u = i t + 1 y_{u}=i_{t+1} the held out next item. A candidate generator x x uses h u h_{u} to produce the ranked list L x k ​ ( u ) = ( i x , u ( 1 ) , … , i x , u ( k ) ) , L_{x}^{k}(u)=\bigl(i_{x,u}^{(1)},\ldots,i_{x,u}^{(k)}\bigr), where i x , u ( j ) i_{x,u}^{(j)} is the item at rank j j . Models We compare GR and DR using the TIGER and LIGER framework ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Both arms use the same interaction data, item catalog, and jointly trained T5 encoder decoder. GR decodes valid semantic IDs through prefix constrained beam search, while DR ranks items by cosine similarity using the encoder representation of the same history. Thus, the arms differ mainly in their retrieval readout. Datasets Our public evaluation uses the 2014 and 2023 releases of Amazon Toys. The 2014 dataset contains 11,924 items and 19,412 user histories under a leave last out split. Among their held out targets, 19,116 were seen during training and 296 were absent from training. Our results reproduce the LIGER Recall@10 values, while our GR recall exceeds the published TIGER result. The 2023 catalog is 13.6 × 13.6\times larger, which tests whether the observed pattern and the proposed intervention survive a substantial increase in catalog scale ( Hou et al., 2024 ) . We transfer the value weights and reranking coefficient from 2014 to 2023 without change unless stated otherwise. 4. Evaluation Metrics We compare GR and DR by asking which retrieved items are relevant and how much value they carry . A relevance labeling rule q u ​ ( i ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q_{u}(i)\in[0,1] assigns evaluation credit after ranking and is not a model score. It may credit only the held-out item, include substitute candidates, or assign partial credit through graded judgments. In contrast, v i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] v_{i}\in[0,1] measures a static property of item i i . For any rule q q , the relevant set with k k candidates is defined as R x k ​ ( u , q ) = { i ∈ L x k ​ ( u ) ∣ q u ​ ( i ) > 0 } . R_{x}^{k}(u;q)=\{i\in L_{x}^{k}(u)\mid q_{u}(i)>0\}. This definition keeps relevance and item value separate across evaluation protocols. In this section, We first define exact-target and category-based relevance, then introduce static catalog value, and finally combine them at the best-item and whole-list levels. 4.1. Exact-Target Retrieval The conventional next item protocol assigns credit only to the held out item, as defined by q u exact ( i ) = 𝟙 [ i = y u ] q_{u}^{\mathrm{exact}}(i)=\mathds{1}[i=y_{u}] . Recall@ k k measures whether this item appears in the top- k k results. Recall x @ k = 1 | 𝒰 | ∑ u ∈ 𝒰 𝟙 [ y u ∈ L x k ( u ) ] . \mathrm{Recall}_{x}@k=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathds{1}[y_{u}\in L_{x}^{k}(u)]. NDCG@ k k evaluates the same target with a rank discount ( Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002 ) . Both metrics measure recovery of the observed next interaction and give no credit to other potentially useful items. 4.2. Beyond Exact Match: Substitute Blindness Exact target evaluation cannot distinguish a substitute from an irrelevant item because both receive zero credit. We refer to this limitation as substitute blindness . A larger substitute set | S ⁡ ( u ) | |S(u)| makes an exact miss less informative, but category overlap alone does not establish that two items are substitutes. We therefore stress-test this proxy using co-purchase credit, a mass-matched random-credit control, and LLM-judged graded relevance in Section 6 . 4.3. Static Item Value Relevance determines whether an item is useful for a given user. In e-commerce, products also differ in static catalog attributes that may matter to the platform. We summarize these attributes with a transparent item-value proxy (1) v i ​ ( 𝐰 ) = w p ​ pop i + w r ​ rate i + w b ​ brand i , w p + w r + w b = 1 . v_{i}(\mathbf{w})=w_{p}\,\mathrm{pop}_{i}+w_{r}\,\mathrm{rate}_{i}+w_{b}\,\mathrm{brand}_{i},\quad w_{p}+w_{r}+w_{b}=1. All weights are nonnegative. Unless otherwise stated, we use the default weights 𝐰 = ( 0.25 , 0.25 , 0.50 ) \mathbf{w}=(0.25,0.25,0.50) . Conditional best-item value (BV) BV asks how valuable the best relevant item returned by method x x is for user u u . From Metric Dependency to a Static Prior We now apply these complementary metrics in a three-step analysis. We first show that GR leads on BV while DR leads on vNDCG \mathrm{vNDCG} . We then measure how popularity, rating, and brand contribute to GR’s value advantage. Finally, we rerank DR with the same static item value and test whether the gap reverses. 5.1. The Metric-Dependent GR–DR Gap We begin with the empirical disagreement. GR leads on BV, while raw DR leads on vNDCG ​ @ ​ 50 \mathrm{vNDCG}@50 , Recall@50, and target NDCG@50 on both datasets as shown in Table 1 . GR wins the paired BV comparison more than twice as often as raw DR (Figure 2 (a)), and its lead remains when users without a relevant retrieved item receive zero. DR’s vNDCG ​ @ ​ 50 \mathrm{vNDCG}@50 lead is 2.9% in 2014 and 5.1% in 2023, with confidence intervals above zero (Figure 2 (b)). Value weighting compresses DR’s relevance advantage by an order of magnitude. We conduct a full sweep on value weights to demonstrate robustness. Across the 231-point weight simplex shown in Fig. 3 , the sign of the vNDCG \mathrm{vNDCG} gap holds on 223 points on 2014, failing only in popularity-dominated edge cases, and on all 231 points on 2023. Figure 2. Metric choice reverses the result. (a) GR wins more often under BV ​ @ ​ 50 \mathrm{BV}@50 in both datasets. (b) Under vNDCG ​ @ ​ 50 \mathrm{vNDCG}@50 , DR scores higher than GR and DR+prior scores highest. Error bars show standard errors for adjacent differences. 5.2. Diagnosing GR’s Value Advantage Among users where GR wins BV \mathrm{BV} , we use Equation 1 to break its value lead over DR into popularity, rating, and brand. Popularity contributes for 49.8% of the lead on 2014 and 65.4% on 2023. It is the largest component on both datasets, and its share is higher on the larger 2023 catalog. Rating and brand contribute the remainder, but neither provides the same cross-dataset dominance. This pattern narrows the interpretation of GR’s value edge. Each value component is computed once per item and does not depend on the current history. The measured lift is therefore largely captured by static item-level properties, especially popularity. Repeated exposure in training offers a possible explanation for GR’s value lead. The released 2014 popularity score correlates with how often held out targets appear in training histories (Spearman ρ = 0.582 \rho=0.582 ). At least ten training histories contain 50.3% of held out targets in 2014 and 75.1% in 2023. GR may learn a preference for frequently seen items while predicting their semantic IDs. This could contribute to its lead because popularity is part of the item value score. That statement yields a falsifiable implication. If static item properties account for the operational advantage, then explicitly adding the same information to DR should reproduce it without autoregressive decoding. 5.3. Conclusion In this paper, we revisited the GR and DR in a controlled e-commerce comparison and we find two distinct parts to GR’s measured advantage. First, metric choice changes the apparent winner. GR leads on the value of the best relevant item, while DR leads on exact target recall and relevant value across the ranked list on both public datasets. Second, popularity makes the largest contribution to GR’s value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this gap while preserving DR’s recall lead. Cold target and substitute credit checks do not reveal a broader GR advantage. Graded judgments on an industrial dataset place DR above a larger GR model and DR with the prior above both. These results make DR with a static value prior a useful baseline for future GR systems. References Abdollahpouri et al. (2019) H. Abdollahpouri, M. Mansoury, R. Burke, and B.
